name: Kolkata
info: Kolkata, known as Calcutta until 2001, is a city on the Hooghly River in eastern India, grown from three villages after the East India Company settled there in 1690, and the capital of British India until 1911.

facts.founded: The recorded history of the city began in 1690 with the arrival of the English East India Company. Job Charnock is often regarded as the founder, but in 2003 the Calcutta High Court ruled that the city has no founder.
facts.where: On the eastern bank of the Hooghly River in the lower Ganges Delta, in West Bengal, India, about 80 km west of the border with Bangladesh.
facts.known: The Company settlement of Calcutta; the siege of 1756 and the Black Hole; the Battle of Plassey; capital of British India until 1911; the Bengal Renaissance; the University of Calcutta; the nationalist movement; the Partition of 1947
facts.today: Kolkata is the capital of the Indian state of West Bengal and the largest city of eastern India.

t: Three villages on the Hooghly became the English East India Company's settlement from 1690, and after the Company's victory at Plassey in 1757 Calcutta was the centre of its rule in Bengal.
As the capital of British India until 1911 it grew into the second largest city of the British Empire after London and was the home of the Bengal Renaissance and of the early nationalist movement.
The famine of 1943, the communal violence of 1946 and the Partition of 1947 changed its population, and later decades brought economic decline and then recovery.
dyk: The Calcutta High Court ruled in 2003 that Job Charnock, long believed to be the founder of Calcutta, was not its founder, and that the city therefore has no birthday.
ev: Job Charnock returns to Sutanuti and hoists the Company standard on the bank of the Hooghly
Siraj ud-Daulah captures Calcutta and Fort William
The Company defeats the Nawab at Plassey, and Calcutta becomes the centre of its power in Bengal
A cyclone strikes the city and kills about 60,000 people
The capital of British India moves from Calcutta to New Delhi
Millions starve in the Bengal famine
The partition of India and of Bengal sends hundreds of thousands of Hindus into the city
The city's official name changes from Calcutta to Kolkata

sections.origins:
Kolkata lies on the eastern bank of the Hooghly River in the lower Ganges Delta, about 80 km west of the border with Bangladesh. Much of the city was originally wetland that was reclaimed over the decades. Excavations at Chandraketugarh, 35 km to the north, show that the region has been inhabited for over two millennia. The village of Kalikata is first mentioned in Bipradas Pipilai's Manasa Vijay of 1495, in which the merchant Chand Sadagar stops at Kalighat to worship the goddess Kali on a trading voyage, and again in Mukundaram Chakrabarti's Chandimangal of 1594 and in Todar Mal's taxation list of 1596.

The site of the present city held three villages: Kalikata, a fishing village; Sutanuti, a village of riverside weavers; and Gobindapur, a trading post for Indian merchants. They belonged to an estate of the Sabarna Roy Choudhury family of zamindars, under the Nawab of Bengal and Mughal suzerainty. The name Kolkata comes from Kôlikata, the Bengali name of Kalikata. Proposed origins include the Bengali Kalikshetra, the "field of Kali", the nearby Kalighat, the word kilkila for a flat area, and the village's trade in quicklime and coir.

The Company's agent Job Charnock settled at Sutanuti in 1690, and the city's recorded history is dated from then. He is often called its founder, but the Calcutta High Court ruled in 2003 that the city has none.
sections.growth:
The Company completed Fort William on the east bank of the Hooghly to protect its trading factory, and after 1757 the city became the centre of its control over Bengal. Calcutta had a population of 120,000 in 1750. Under Richard Wellesley, Governor-General from 1797 to 1805, the marshes round the city were drained, the government area was laid out along the river and its public architecture was built. The city was a centre of the Company's opium trade, in which opium bought from local traders and farmers was sold at auction in Calcutta, and much of it was then smuggled to Canton.

A census of 1837 recorded 229,700 people in the city proper, of whom 3,138 were British, and a further 177,000 in the suburbs and neighbouring villages. From the early 1850s Calcutta industrialised rapidly, above all in textiles and jute, and British companies invested in telegraph lines and in Howrah. The Port of Kolkata was established in 1870. In the 19th century Calcutta was called the second city of the British Empire after London. The city also became a centre of learning, with the Asiatic Society of Bengal founded in 1784, the Calcutta Medical College in 1835 and the University of Calcutta in 1857.
sections.rulers:
From the 14th to the 16th century the area was under the Bengal Sultanate, and the Mughal Empire incorporated it into the Bengal Subah in 1576. The three villages were then ruled by the Nawab of Bengal under Mughal suzerainty. The Mughal emperor granted the East India Company freedom of trade in return for an annual payment of 3,000 rupees.

Nawab Siraj ud-Daulah took the city in 1756 and renamed it Alinagar, and the Company retook it in January 1757. After Plassey in 1757 Mir Jafar was made Nawab and the Company controlled Bengal in effect. By the Treaty of Allahabad of 1765 the Company became tax collector for the Mughal emperor in Bengal, Bihar and Orissa, while Mughal-appointed Nawabs continued to rule the province. Calcutta was declared a presidency city and had become the Company's headquarters by 1773. In 1793 the power of the Nawabs was abolished and the Company took complete control of the city and province.

Calcutta served as the de facto capital of India under the Company and later the Crown until 1911, when the capital moved to New Delhi. After independence in 1947 it became the capital of the Indian state of West Bengal. From 1977 to 2011 the state was governed from Kolkata by the Left Front, led by the Communist Party of India (Marxist), and the Trinamool Congress succeeded it in 2011.
sections.life:
By the 1850s Calcutta had two areas: White Town, mainly British and centred on Chowringhee and Dalhousie Square, and Black Town, mainly Indian and centred on North Calcutta. Unions between Europeans and local Hindu and Muslim women were common in the 18th century and are the origin of the city's Anglo-Indian community, but by the early 19th century increasing racial intolerance made them much rarer. Alongside the British lived Bengali Hindus, who formed the majority, Marwaris, Biharis, Urdu-speaking Muslims and smaller communities of Chinese, Armenians, Greeks, Jews and others. Once home to 20,000 ethnic Chinese, the city's Chinatown fell to around 2,000 people, partly after the Sino-Indian War of 1962.

Contact between British and Indian culture produced the babu class of urbane Indians, often bureaucrats, professionals and newspaper readers, usually from upper-caste Hindu communities, and the Bengal Renaissance of the 19th century. Hickey's Bengal Gazette, printed from 29 January 1780, was the first newspaper in India. The Government College of Art and Craft was founded in 1864, and Kalighat painting arose in 19th-century Kolkata. The city developed neighbourhoods with a strong sense of community, called paras, and the leisurely, freestyle conversation known as adda. In the 19th and 20th centuries writers including Bankim Chandra Chatterjee and Rabindranath Tagore modernised Bengali literature.
sections.crises:
In 1756 the Company began to strengthen the fortifications of Fort William during its rivalry with the French, which angered Nawab Siraj ud-Daulah. He captured Cossimbazar and then Calcutta, which fell on 20 June 1756 after a short siege. The governor and many officials escaped down the river, leaving the rest of the garrison and the Eurasian population. Several Company officials were killed in what became known as the Black Hole of Calcutta. It is said that 123 Britons died there, but recent evidence calls the numbers into question. The Company recaptured the city on 2 January 1757. Cyclones struck in 1737 and 1864 and killed thousands, and the cyclone of 5 October 1864 killed about 60,000 people. The city and its port were bombed several times by the Japanese between 1942 and 1944.

Millions starved to death in the Bengal famine of 1943, which came from a combination of military, administrative and natural factors. Demands for a Muslim state led in 1946 to communal violence in which over 4,000 people were killed. The partition of India led to further clashes: many Muslims left for East Bengal, and hundreds of thousands of Hindus fled into the city. In the 1960s and 1970s power shortages, strikes and the violent Naxalite movement damaged much of its infrastructure, and in 1971 refugees from East Pakistan strained it further.
sections.legacy:
Calcutta was the centre of the early nationalist movement. In 1883 it hosted the first national conference of the Indian National Association, the first avowed nationalist organisation in India, and the partition of Bengal in 1905 along religious lines led to mass protests. The revolutionary organisations Jugantar and Anushilan Samiti were formed there, and Bankim Chandra Chattopadhyay wrote the song Vande Mataram. Subhas Chandra Bose escaped from his Elgin Road house in Calcutta to reach Germany during the Second World War. In 1971 the city was home to the government-in-exile of Bangladesh.

The University of Calcutta was the first modern university in South Asia, and the Indian Museum, established in 1814, is the country's oldest museum. Among the city's imperial buildings are the Victoria Memorial and the Howrah Bridge. Rabindranath Tagore, C. V. Raman and Amartya Sen are among the Nobel laureates associated with it, and Mother Teresa received the Nobel Peace Prize for the Missionaries of Charity, which she founded there. Mumbai overtook it as India's most populous city in the mid-1980s, and its economy recovered after the 1990s. The official name changed from Calcutta to Kolkata in 2001. Kolkata is now the capital of West Bengal, with about 4.5 million people in the city proper and over 14 million in its urban agglomeration.

summary: Kolkata, called Calcutta until 2001, grew from three villages on the Hooghly after the East India Company settled there in 1690. It was the capital of British India until 1911 and a centre of the Bengal Renaissance and the nationalist movement. It is now the capital of West Bengal.
references: Sukanta Chaudhuri, Calcutta, the Living City: The past (Oxford University Press, 1990)
Swati Chattopadhyay, Representing Calcutta: Modernity, Nationalism, and the Colonial Uncanny (Psychology Press, 2005)
Anindita Ghosh, Claiming the City: Protest, Crime, and Scandals in Colonial Calcutta, c. 1860–1920 (Oxford University Press, 2016)
Tanika Sarkar, Calcutta: The Stormy Decades (Social Science Press, 2015)
Ranabir Ray Choudhury, A City in the Making: Aspects of Calcutta's Early Growth (Niyogi Books, 2016)
notes: FORT WILLIAM: the city article says the British completed Fort William in 1712; the history article says the fort was built from 1695 onwards and completed ca 1701 (and elsewhere dates beginnings to 1698). I left the fort's date out and kept only that it was completed.

PURCHASE OF THE VILLAGES: the city article says the Sabarna Roy Choudhury estate was sold to the Company in 1698; the history article says the Company bought the three villages in 1690. I wrote no year and no purchase date.

START: 1690 is the date both articles give for the Company's arrival; the history article dates the settlement's return to Sutanuti on 24 August 1690, and the High Court says the city's genesis lies in the Maurya and Gupta period, which I left out as unsupported by a date.

CAPITAL: the city article says de facto capital until 1911; the history article says capital of British India from 1772 and of all Bengal from 1912 to 1947. I used only the 1911 move and omitted 1772 and 1912.

BLACK HOLE: the history article says 'it is said that 123 Britons later died'; the city article says only that several officials were killed. I gave both, hedged. The 1756 siege date (20 June) and the 1757 recapture date (2 January) are from the history article only.
PLASSEY: the city article says Siraj ud-Daulah was defeated after Mir Jafar mutinied; the history article gives 23 June 1757 and troop numbers, which I left out.

FAMINE: the causes are given in the article's own words: 'a combination of military, administrative, and natural factors'. The article does not say how many died in the city itself, only 'millions' (Bengal famine).

1864 CYCLONE: both articles say about 60,000 died; the history article gives the date 5 October 1864 and says the city was 'almost destroyed'. The city article says 'about 60,000 in Kolkata'. 1737 cyclone: 'thousands', no figure.

POPULATION: 120,000 in 1750 and the 1837 census figures as given; the history article's '117,000 to 1,098,000' over 150 years has no clear start year and was left out. Modern figures: 4,496,694 (2011 census, city) and 14,112,536 (urban agglomeration, 2011), written as 'about 4.5 million' and 'over 14 million' without the year.

1946 VIOLENCE: 'killed over 4,000' is the city article's figure; the history article says only that communal relations 'savaged Calcutta in 1946 and 1947'. No perpetrators or victims are named by either article.

CHINATOWN: 20,000 once, around 2,000 'as of 2009'; the 1962 war is one of several factors in the article ('repatriation and denial of Indian citizenship following the 1962 Sino-Indian War, and emigration'). I wrote 'partly after the Sino-Indian War of 1962'.

Left out: the Japanese bombing dates are as given; the opium trade's link to the First Opium War, the Nanda Kumar trial, the greater adjutant stork, the Asiatic Society's Indo-European work, sport, transport, economy tables and the 1737 detail were omitted for space or as outside the brief.
